a: The vision of Isaiah son of Amoz
t: A vision that is also words
p: Chazon, 'vision', is the heading of the whole book. What Isaiah 'saw' is mostly what he heard and spoke.
b: Chazon comes from chazah, 'see', and it heads the whole book as a title, like the headings of Obadiah 1 and Nahum 1:1. The vision is mostly made of words: 2:1 speaks of 'the word that Isaiah saw'. The prophet's name, Yesha'yahu, means 'the LORD saves', a fitting name for a book about the LORD's salvation. His father Amoz ('Amots) is not the prophet Amos ('Amos), whose name is spelled differently in Hebrew. A rabbinic tradition makes Amoz the brother of King Amaziah, so that Isaiah was of royal blood (Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 10b), but the Bible says nothing of his family beyond his wife and sons (7:3; 8:3).

a: Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah
t: Four kings and the rise of Assyria
p: The heading spans about 60 years, from Uzziah's long reign to Hezekiah's, the years Assyria conquered the west.
b: Uzziah (also called Azariah) reigned about 792–740 BC, counting years shared with his father; in his last years he had a skin disease and his son Jotham governed for him (2 Kings 15:5). Ahaz (about 735–715) asked Assyria for help against Aram and Israel and became its vassal (2 Kings 16:7). Hezekiah (about 715–686) rebelled against Assyria and saw Sennacherib invade in 701 (2 Kings 18–20). These are Edwin Thiele's dates, used throughout this site; other systems, such as that of Hayes and Hooker, differ by up to about twenty years. Over Isaiah's lifetime Tiglath-pileser III (745–727) and his successors turned Assyria into an empire that swallowed Aram (732) and the northern kingdom of Israel (722). The heading leaves out Manasseh, under whom tradition says Isaiah died.

a: Hear, you heavens! Listen, earth!
p: The LORD calls the same witnesses Moses called when Israel took on the covenant.
b: Ancient treaties called the gods as witnesses. Israel's covenant called heaven and earth instead (Deuteronomy 4:26; Deuteronomy 30:19), and the Song of Moses opens the same way: "let the earth hear what my mouth says" (Deuteronomy 32:1). Isaiah 1 is often called a covenant lawsuit (Hebrew riv): the LORD summons witnesses, states his charge (1:2–9), rejects Israel's defense (1:10–15) and offers terms (1:16–20). Huffmon described the pattern in 1959; others, such as Daniels, doubt that prophets used a fixed lawsuit form, but agree that the language of the court runs through the chapter (1:17–18, 23; 3:13–14).

a: For the LORD has spoken
p: Capital letters stand for God's name, YHWH, which Jews do not say aloud.
b: The Hebrew has the four letters YHWH, the personal name of Israel's God (Exodus 3:14–15). Jewish readers say Adonai, 'Lord', in its place, and most English Bibles follow by printing "the LORD" in capitals. Where the Hebrew has Adonai or ha'adon, 'the Lord', this translation prints "Lord" in lower case (1:24; 3:17; 6:1), and where the two stand together, Adonai YHWH, it prints "the Lord GOD" (3:15).

a: Children I have raised and lifted high
p: God speaks as a father whose grown sons have turned on him, a case the law treated with great seriousness.
b: The LORD is Israel's father elsewhere too: "Israel is my son, my firstborn" (Exodus 4:22), and Moses asks, "Isn't he your father, who brought you into being" (Deuteronomy 32:6). The verb for 'rebelled', pasha', is used of a vassal breaking with his overlord (2 Kings 1:1; 8:20). Many commentators hear behind the verse the law of the stubborn and rebellious son, whose parents brought him to the elders (Deuteronomy 21:18–21): the case is grave, yet the father in 1:18–20 still pleads.

a: An ox knows the one who owns it
t: The ox and the donkey at the manger
p: This verse is why Christmas scenes put an ox and a donkey beside the manger.
b: The point is plain: dumb animals know who feeds them, and Israel does not know its God. Luke's Gospel mentions a manger but no animals (Luke 2:7). Christians early on read this verse, with the Greek of Habakkuk 3:2 ('between two living creatures you will be known'), as a sign that the beasts recognized the newborn Lord; the Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew (chapter 14) puts the two animals at the manger and cites both verses. From there the ox and donkey entered Christian art and every nativity scene.
l: Ox and donkey in the nativity

a: my people do not stop to think
t: Not knowing and not paying attention
p: Israel's problem is not lack of information but refusing to consider what it knows.
b: Hitbonen means to look closely, consider, pay attention. Knowing God (yada') in the prophets is more than knowing facts: it is the loyal recognition a servant gives a master, or a vassal a king. Isaiah returns to it: "my people go off into exile: / they have no knowledge" (5:13), and the coming age is one in which the earth is full of the knowledge of the LORD (11:9). Hosea makes the same charge against the north (Hosea 4:1, 6).

a: Woe to
p: Hoy was what mourners cried over a body. A prophet's "Woe!" announces a death that has not happened yet.
b: Hoy was the cry of mourners at a funeral, "Alas, my brother!" (1 Kings 13:30; Jeremiah 22:18). When a prophet cries "Woe to" a living nation, he is mourning it in advance: its conduct has already doomed it. Isaiah uses the word often, above all in the six woes of 5:8–23 and in chapters 28–33. In 1:24 the same word becomes a threat, "Ha!", and in 55:1 a friendly call. This translation renders it "Woe to" before the people addressed.

a: a family of wrongdoers
p: Literally 'a seed of evildoers'. The book ends its first vision with a different seed: 'a holy seed' (6:13).
b: Zera' means seed, offspring, family line. 'A seed of evildoers' is set against the 'holy seed' of 6:13, the stump left after judgment, and the theme of the seed runs to the end of the book (65:9, 23; 66:22). The four phrases of the verse (nation, people, seed, children) move from the largest group to the closest family tie, so that the last word, 'children', echoes the father's complaint in 1:2.

a: the Holy One of Israel
p: Twenty-five times in Isaiah, in both halves of the book, and only a handful of times elsewhere.
b: The title qedosh Yisra'el is Isaiah's signature. It comes 12 times in chapters 1–39 and 13 times in 40–66, and elsewhere only in 2 Kings 19:22 (in Isaiah's own oracle), three psalms (Psalm 71:22; Psalm 78:41; Psalm 89:18) and Jeremiah 50:29 and 51:5. It joins two ideas: the LORD is holy, utterly other and pure (6:3), and yet he binds himself to one people. Scholars of every view see the title as one of the strongest threads tying the book together; those who hold to several authors see it as the mark of a school that kept Isaiah's language.

a: they have turned into outsiders and gone backward
t: Outsiders to God, outsiders in the land
p: Nazoru: 'they have made themselves outsiders'. In 1:7 'outsiders' devour their land.
b: The rare verb nazoru is from zur, the root of zar, 'outsider, stranger'. The people have made themselves outsiders to their own God, and three verses later zarim, 'outsiders', eat their fields (1:7). The punishment fits the sin. The Greek ends the verse at 'they provoked the Holy One of Israel' and has nothing for this line.

a: Where can you be struck next
p: 'Al meh can mean 'Why?' or 'On what (place)?'. The next verse suggests the second: the body is beaten all over.
b: Most older versions read 'al meh as 'Why should you be struck again?' (KJV). It can also mean 'on what?', that is, 'on what part of you could you still be struck?', and verse 6 supports that reading: from foot to head there is no unhurt spot left. Either way the picture is the same: a nation beaten again and again, still refusing to stop its revolt (sarah, turning away). Many think the beating describes Sennacherib's invasion of 701 BC (see 1:8).
orig: עַל מֶה תֻכּוּ עוֹד (al meh tukku 'od)

a: bruises and welts
p: Chabburah, 'welt', is the word of 53:5, 'by his welts'. Christian readers have long linked the two.
b: The three words build a picture of untreated injuries: petsa', a bruise or wound; chabburah, a welt or stripe left by a beating; and makkah teriyyah, a fresh, raw blow. The second word returns in the fourth servant song, where healing comes through the servant's welts (53:5). In chapter 1 no one treats the wounds; in chapter 53 the wounds of one bring healing to many. The remedies named, pressing out, binding and soothing with oil, were the medicine of the day (Luke 10:34).
orig: פֶּצַע וְחַבּוּרָה וּמַכָּה טְרִיָּה (petsa' vechabburah umakkah teriyyah)

a: like a land that outsiders overthrew
t: Overthrown by outsiders, or like Sodom?
p: 'Overthrow' (mahpekhah) is the word used for Sodom's end. Many scholars think the verse first read 'like the overthrow of Sodom'.
b: The noun mahpekhah appears almost only in the phrase 'the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah': "It will be like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah" (Deuteronomy 29:23; also Amos 4:11; Jeremiah 49:18). Since Sodom is named two verses later (1:9–10), many scholars propose that a copyist wrote zarim, 'outsiders', for Sedom, picking it up from earlier in the verse. No manuscript reads 'Sodom', and the Hebrew as it stands makes good sense, so this translation keeps it.

a: like a city hemmed in
t: Jerusalem alone in a ruined land
p: Sennacherib boasted that he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem 'like a bird in a cage' after taking 46 towns.
b: Most scholars date 1:4–9 to 701 BC. Sennacherib's annals (on the Taylor and Chicago prisms) claim that he besieged and took 46 walled towns of Judah and countless villages, deported many people, and shut up Hezekiah in Jerusalem 'like a bird in a cage'. Jerusalem survived, alone, like a watchman's hut left standing in a stripped field. Some date the oracle instead to the Syro-Ephraimite invasion of 734 BC (2 Kings 16:5), but 701 fits the size of the devastation best. The booth (sukkah) and the shack were flimsy shelters for those guarding crops at harvest.

a: Daughter Zion
p: Bat Tsiyyon pictures Jerusalem as a young woman. It does not mean 'the daughter of Zion' as if Zion had a child.
b: The Hebrew bat Tsiyyon is a common way of speaking of a city as a woman: Zion herself is the daughter. The same phrase appears in Isaiah's taunt to Sennacherib, where "the virgin, Daughter Zion" laughs at the Assyrian (2 Kings 19:21; 37:22). In Isaiah the city is in turn a faithful wife turned prostitute (1:21), a widow on the ground (3:26), a mother bereaved and then given children (49:14–21), and a bride (62:4–5).

a: the LORD of Armies
p: YHWH tseva'ot, 'the LORD of hosts'. 'Armies' may mean Israel's armies, the angels or the stars.
b: This is the first of more than fifty uses of YHWH tseva'ot in Isaiah; only Jeremiah has more. Tseva'ot means armies or hosts. It may refer to Israel's armies (1 Samuel 17:45), to the angels (1 Kings 22:19) or to the stars (40:26), and the title probably came to include them all: the LORD commands every power in heaven and on earth. The CSB and WEB likewise have 'of Armies'; the KJV and ESV have 'of hosts', the NIV 'Almighty'. The Greek of Isaiah keeps the Hebrew word, kyrios sabaoth, and Paul's quotation of this verse does too (Romans 9:29).
orig: יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת (YHWH tseva'ot); Greek κύριος σαβαώθ (kyrios sabaōth)

a: we would have become like Sodom
t: Paul and the few who were left
p: Paul quotes this verse, in the Greek, to show that God always keeps a remnant of Israel (Romans 9:29).
b: In Romans 9:27–29 Paul joins two passages of Isaiah: 10:22–23, that only a remnant will return, and this verse, in the Greek's wording, 'If the Lord of Sabaoth had not left us a seed'. For Paul the 'seed' that God kept is the believing remnant of Israel in his own day, a sign that God's word has not failed (Romans 9:6; 11:5). For Isaiah, the survivors are the people of Jerusalem left after the invasion: not a reward for their goodness, but God's mercy alone. Sodom and Gomorrah, destroyed with no survivors (Genesis 19:24–25), are the measure of what Judah deserved.

a: you rulers of Sodom
p: Isaiah turns the comparison of 1:9 into an accusation: the leaders are not just like Sodom's survivors, they are Sodom's rulers.
b: In 1:9 the people would have been like Sodom in their fate; in 1:10 their rulers are like Sodom in their conduct. Ezekiel names Sodom's sin as pride, plenty and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49), and Isaiah's charge in this chapter is the same: blood on the hands and no justice for orphans and widows (1:15–17, 23). The comparison returns in 3:9. Revelation calls Jerusalem, 'where their Lord was crucified', 'spiritually Sodom' (Revelation 11:8).

a: the teaching of our God
p: Torah means teaching or instruction. In Isaiah it is usually what God or the prophet teaches, set beside 'the LORD's word'.
b: Torah comes from yarah, 'to point the way, teach'. In the books of Moses it is often a body of law, and older English Bibles always render it 'law'. In Isaiah it usually means instruction given by God through a prophet or priest, as here, where it stands in parallel with "the LORD's word". So this translation uses "teaching" (also 2:3; 5:24; 8:16, 20; 30:9). What follows in 1:11–17 is a teaching about worship, given by a prophet, not a quotation of the written law. Jewish readers also hear the written Torah in the word.

a: What use to me are all your many sacrifices?
p: Isaiah, Amos, Hosea, Micah and Jeremiah all attack sacrifice. Most readers think they attack sacrifice without justice.
b: Some nineteenth-century scholars read 1:11–15 as a rejection of the whole sacrificial system. Most now think the prophets attacked worship that was used as a cover for injustice: Isaiah goes on to reject prayer too (1:15), and no one thinks he was against prayer. The issue is the blood on the hands that are raised (1:15). Samuel had already said that "listening is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:22), and the Psalms make the same point (Psalm 50:13–14; Psalm 51:16–17). Jewish and Christian readers agree that the passage is about the heart and about justice; Christians have also read it as preparing for the end of animal sacrifice (Hebrews 10:4–10).
r: Amos 5:21–24; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6–8; Jeremiah 7:21–23; 1 Samuel 15:22; Psalm 50:13–14; Psalm 51:16–17; Hebrews 10:4–10

a: When you come to be seen before me
t: To see God's face, or to appear before him?
p: The letters can mean 'to see my face'. The vowels the Masoretes added make it 'to appear before me'.
b: Israel's festival law tells every male to 'appear before the LORD' three times a year (Exodus 23:17; 34:23–24; Deuteronomy 16:16). In all these places the Hebrew letters could be read 'to see the face of the LORD', which is probably the older meaning: a pilgrim went to the Temple to 'see God's face'. The Masoretes, who added the vowels to the text in the early Middle Ages, read them as a passive, 'to be seen', perhaps out of reverence, since no one can see God and live (Exodus 33:20). Isaiah himself will 'see' the Lord in 6:1, 5.

a: New Moon and Sabbath
p: Two festivals often named together in the 700s BC. On both, work and trade stopped.
b: The New Moon, the first day of each month, was a feast day with extra sacrifices (Numbers 28:11–15) and a family meal (1 Samuel 20:5, 18). In the 700s BC it is regularly named beside the Sabbath (2 Kings 4:23; Amos 8:5; Hosea 2:11). Amos describes merchants who could not wait for either day to end so they could cheat again (Amos 8:5). Isaiah's last chapter returns to both days: then all people will come to worship 'from New Moon to New Moon, and from Sabbath to Sabbath' (66:23).

a: Blood fills your hands
p: Israelites prayed standing, with palms spread open toward heaven. The hands God sees are stained with blood.
b: To 'spread out the palms' was the gesture of prayer (1 Kings 8:22, 38; Psalm 143:6). The blood on those hands is not the blood of sacrifices but of violence and injustice: the city that was faithful is now full of 'killers' (1:21). The Hebrew has the plural damim, 'bloods', which in the Bible usually means bloodshed and blood-guilt. Paul may echo the image when he asks men to pray 'lifting up holy hands without anger' (1 Timothy 2:8).

a: Wash yourselves, become clean
t: Washing that changes how one lives
p: The priests' language of washing becomes a call to stop doing evil. Early Christians read it of baptism.
b: Israel's purity laws called for washing with water (Leviticus 14:8–9; 15:5). Here the washing is moral, and the following commands explain it: stop doing evil, learn to do good, seek justice. The psalmist asks the same: "Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow" (Psalm 51:7), and Psalm 24 asks for "Someone whose hands are clean and whose heart is pure" (Psalm 24:4). Justin Martyr, about AD 155, quoted 1:16–20 when he explained Christian baptism to the Roman emperor (First Apology 61; he also quotes it on free will in 44).

a: Put the ruthless in their place
t: Correct the oppressor, or help the oppressed?
p: The rare word chamots may mean 'the ruthless one' or 'the one wronged'. Translations go both ways.
b: 'Ashru chamots is hard. Chamots appears only here; related words mean 'violent' or 'sour'. Read as 'the oppressor', the line says: set the ruthless straight (correct the oppressor). Read as 'the oppressed', as the Greek ('rescue the one wronged'), the Latin and the KJV ('relieve the oppressed') take it, the line says: lead the downtrodden to safety. The verb 'ishsher can mean 'lead, set straight' or 'call happy'. The sense of the whole verse is clear either way: justice for the weak.

a: Give the orphan his rights
p: Without a father or husband to speak for them in court, orphans and widows could lose everything.
b: In Israel a man spoke for his household at the town gate, where cases were tried. A widow or a fatherless child had no one, so the law put them under God's own protection: "Never treat a widow or a fatherless child harshly" (Exodus 22:22). The prophets measured a city's justice by them (1:23; 10:2; Jeremiah 7:6; Zechariah 7:10), and so does the New Testament (James 1:27). 'Give the orphan his rights' is literally 'judge the orphan', that is, give him a fair hearing.

a: let us argue it out
p: 'Let us reason together' (KJV) sounds like a calm discussion. The Hebrew is the language of a courtroom.
b: Nokhechah is from yakhach, 'argue a case, decide, set right' (2:4 'set things right'). It continues the lawsuit begun in 1:2: the plaintiff invites the accused to settle the case. The KJV's 'let us reason together' is accurate in older English, but today it suggests a polite conversation between equals. The offer that follows is serious, and it comes with terms (1:19–20).

a: If your sins are scarlet
t: A promise, a question, or a condition?
p: Most read 1:18 as a promise of cleansing. Some read it as an ironic question, and others as an offer that depends on 1:19–20.
b: Three readings are held. (1) A promise: God will make the guiltiest clean, the most common reading in Jewish and Christian teaching and in hymns. (2) A question or irony: 'If your sins are scarlet, can they become white as snow?' The Hebrew has no question marker, but questions without one exist; some scholars take it this way because 1:15 has just refused their prayers. (3) A conditional offer: forgiveness is real, but 1:19–20 makes it depend on willingness and obedience. Many readers combine (1) and (3): the offer is free and must be taken.

a: scarlet
p: The red dye came from an insect and did not wash out. That is the point: sins too deep to scrub away.
b: Shani and tola' name the same colorfast red dye, made from the dried bodies of a scale insect that lives on oak trees (the kermes). Tola' means 'worm'. The dye was expensive and was used for the Tabernacle curtains (Exodus 26:1) and royal clothing (2 Samuel 1:24). It was famous for not washing out. Snow and wool are the whitest things an Israelite knew.

a: the sword will eat you
p: A wordplay: if you obey, 'you will eat' (tokhelu, 1:19); if you refuse, 'you will be eaten' (te'ukkelu).
b: Hebrew poets love sound-plays. The good of the land and the sword are both 'eaten' with the same verb: tokhelu, 'you will eat', and te'ukkelu, 'you will be eaten'. The 'mouth' of the sword (its edge, in Hebrew idiom) and 'the LORD's own mouth' in the next line close the case. The formula "The LORD's own mouth has said it" comes again at 40:5 and 58:14, one of many phrases that run through the whole book.

a: How has she turned into a prostitute
t: A funeral song for a city
p: 'Ekhah, 'How!', is how a funeral lament begins. Isaiah sings Jerusalem's dirge while she still stands.
b: 'Ekhah opens Lamentations three times (Lamentations 1:1; 2:1; 4:1). The verses 1:21–26 are a little poem in the shape of a ring: 'faithful town' in 1:21 and 1:26, justice and righteousness in 1:21 and 1:26–27, the city's leaders in 1:23 and its judges in 1:26. The prostitute is a picture of unfaithfulness to God, as in Hosea 1–3, Jeremiah 3 and Ezekiel 16; here the unfaithfulness is chiefly injustice and murder, not the worship of other gods.

a: Your silver has turned into dross
p: The best things in the city, its silver and its wine, have been debased. The image looks ahead to the refining of 1:25.
b: Silver ore was smelted to separate the pure metal from the dross. Jerusalem's silver has become all dross: there is nothing left worth keeping. Watered wine was a merchant's trick, and some read the line literally, as cheating in trade; most read both images as pictures of the city's leaders, once valuable and now worthless. In 1:25 the LORD himself becomes the smelter who refines the dross away, a picture of judgment that purifies rather than destroys (also 48:10; Ezekiel 22:18–22; Malachi 3:2–3).

a: Your officials are rebels
p: Another sound-play: sarayikh sorerim, 'your officials are outlaws'.
b: The officials (sarim) are sorerim, 'stubborn, rebellious', the word Deuteronomy uses of the son who will not obey (Deuteronomy 21:18) and Hosea of the north (Hosea 9:15, where the same play occurs). They take bribes (shochad), which the law forbids: "a bribe blinds those who see clearly" (Exodus 23:8). The result is that the widow's lawsuit 'never gets in to them': it never even comes to court.

a: the Mighty One of Israel
p: A rare old title, used of Jacob's God in Genesis 49:24. Here it is the only time it is 'of Israel'.
b: 'Avir Ya'aqov, 'the Mighty One of Jacob', is one of the oldest titles of God: Jacob blesses Joseph "by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob" (Genesis 49:24; also Psalm 132:2, 5). Isaiah uses it again in 49:26 and 60:16. Only here is it 'of Israel'. The Lord piles up three titles, the Lord (ha'adon, 'the master'), the LORD of Armies and the Mighty One, before he speaks against his own city. 'Declares' renders ne'um, a noun meaning 'an utterance': 'the utterance of the Lord'.

a: Ha! I will ease my heart against my foes
p: 'Enachem is from nacham, 'comfort'. The God who here 'comforts himself' by judging will later say 'Comfort, comfort my people' (40:1).
b: Hoy here is not a lament but a threat: 'Ha!'. The verb 'enachem means 'I will relieve myself, find comfort' (also 'regret, relent' in other forms). God's foes, surprisingly, are his own people: the corrupt rulers of Jerusalem. The same root, nacham, opens the second half of the book: 'Comfort, comfort my people' (40:1), and runs through it (49:13; 51:3, 12; 66:13). The book moves from God comforting himself by judging Zion to God comforting Zion. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads 'his foes ... his enemies', which may be a slip or a change that keeps God from speaking of his own people as his enemies.

a: as lye does
p: Kabbor, 'as with lye', may refer to the alkali added to molten metal. Some emend it to 'in the furnace'.
b: Silver was refined by heating it with lead and an alkali (lye or potash, bor), which drew off the impurities as slag. 'As with lye' fits that process. Some scholars swap two letters to read bakkur, 'in the furnace' (as in 48:10). Bedil, here 'tin', is the base metal mixed into the silver: the metal for the plumb line in Zechariah 4:10. The 'hand' of the LORD turned against his city is a hand of judgment, but its purpose is to purify (1:26).

a: City of Righteousness, Faithful Town
p: Isaiah gives Jerusalem new names more than once. A name in the Bible tells what a thing is.
b: After judgment the city will be what it once was (1:21): faithful and full of righteousness. The prophets often give Jerusalem a new name for its new life: 'the City of the LORD, Zion of the Holy One of Israel' (60:14), 'My Delight Is in Her' (62:4), 'Sought Out, a City Not Forsaken' (62:12), 'The LORD Is Our Righteousness' (Jeremiah 33:16), 'The LORD Is There' (Ezekiel 48:35), 'the City of Truth' (Zechariah 8:3). 'I will bring back your judges' uses the same verb, 'ashivah, as 'I will turn my hand' (1:25): the same hand that strikes restores.

a: Through justice Zion will be ransomed
p: Mishpat and tsedaqah, the pair that sums up what the LORD wants from a city: fair courts and right living.
b: Mishpat (justice) is the right decision of a judge and the order of a just society; tsedaqah (righteousness) is right conduct, faithfulness to what a relationship requires. Together they mean social justice (1:21; 5:7, 16; 9:7; 28:17; 32:16; 33:5). Here they are the means of Zion's ransom (padah, 'buy back, set free'): whose justice? Some read the city's own renewed justice (1:26); others, God's just judgment, which saves those who turn back by removing the rebels (1:28). In 40–66 tsedaqah more often means God's saving action, 'victory' or 'rescue'.

a: The oaks you craved
p: Big trees and garden plots were places of worship for other gods, or for the LORD in forbidden ways.
b: Shady trees on hilltops were places of worship all over Canaan, and Israel was forbidden to worship there: Ahaz "sacrificed and burned offerings at the high places, on the hills and under every leafy tree" (2 Kings 16:4; Deuteronomy 12:2). The 'oaks' ('elim, probably terebinths) and 'gardens' return at the end of the book, where people 'sacrifice in gardens' (65:3; 66:17), another link between the book's first and last chapters. The switch from 'them' to 'you' in the Hebrew is abrupt; some scholars smooth it, but such shifts are common in Hebrew poetry.

a: The strong man will turn into flax fiber
t: The strong one and his work
p: Who is 'the strong one', and what is 'his work'? Perhaps the powerful man and his idol, which burn together.
b: Hechason, 'the strong (one)', may be the powerful man of the city or the strong tree of 1:30. Po'alo, 'his work', may be what he has made, probably an idol, the 'work of their hands' (2:8); the Masoretes' vowels allow 'his maker' too, but 'his work' is the usual reading. Flax tow catches fire at a spark. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads 'your strength' and 'your work', addressing the hearers directly. The final words, 'with no one to put it out', are echoed in the book's last verse (66:24).

a: The word that Isaiah son of Amoz saw
p: A new title in 2:1 shows that chapter 1 was set in front of an older collection, probably chapters 2–12.
b: The book has headings at 1:1, 2:1 and 13:1. Most scholars think 2:1 once introduced a collection of Isaiah's oracles (perhaps chapters 2–4, or 2–12), and that chapter 1 was later placed before it as an introduction to the whole book. Traditional readers see 2:1 as a heading for the vision of Zion that follows. Either way, 'the word that he saw' shows that for the prophets a word could be 'seen'.

a: In the days to come
p: Be'acharit hayyamim can mean 'in the future' or 'at the end of days'. Later Judaism and the New Testament read it as the last age.
b: The phrase is literally 'in the after-part of the days'. In Genesis 49:1 and Numbers 24:14 it means 'in time to come', without necessarily meaning the end of history. In Daniel 10:14 it points to the final age, and the Greek here has 'in the last days', the phrase the New Testament uses for the age that began with Christ (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2) and for the time before his return (2 Timothy 3:1). Jewish tradition reads 2:2–4 of the days of the Messiah. Whatever the timing, the vision is of a future unlike the present.
r: Genesis 49:1; Numbers 24:14; Deuteronomy 4:30; Daniel 10:14; Hosea 3:5; Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2

a: the mountain where the LORD's house stands
p: The same oracle stands in Micah 4:1–3, almost word for word. Who wrote it first is debated.
b: Isaiah 2:2–4 and Micah 4:1–3 are nearly the same in Hebrew. Micah adds a verse of village peace, everyone under his own vine and fig tree (Micah 4:4), and speaks of 'strong nations far away'. Views: (1) Isaiah wrote it and Micah, his younger contemporary, quoted it; (2) Micah wrote it and Isaiah borrowed it; (3) both used an older hymn sung at the Temple; (4) a later editor placed it in both books, perhaps in the exile or after, when hope for the nations' pilgrimage grew. Isaiah's chapter 2 fits it well: the high mountain of 2:2 is the one height left standing when everything else is brought low (2:12–17).

a: will be set firm at the head of the mountains
p: Zion is a small hill. Ancient peoples pictured the home of the gods as the highest mountain; Isaiah sees Zion lifted above all.
b: The Temple hill is lower than the Mount of Olives across the valley. The poem pictures a change in the earth itself: Zion becomes the highest mountain of the world. Canaanite poems from Ugarit place Baal's palace on Mount Zaphon, and a psalm boldly calls Zion "the heights of Zaphon, / the town of the great King" (Psalm 48:2). The idea of a cosmic mountain where heaven meets earth was common; Israel used it to say that the LORD, not Baal, is king of the world. Ezekiel (Ezekiel 40:2) and Revelation (Revelation 21:10) see the same high mountain.

a: and like a river, all the nations will run to it
p: Nahar, 'to stream like a river', and the stream flows up the mountain.
b: The verb nahar comes from the noun for river. Rivers run down mountains; these nations run up one. The picture is of a world turned around: the nations that came against Jerusalem as a flood (8:7–8; 17:12–13) come to it as pilgrims. In Micah 4:1 it is 'peoples'. Later in the book the nations bring Zion's children and their wealth (49:22; 60:3–5), and Zechariah sees ten men from every nation take hold of a Jew's robe (Zechariah 8:23).

a: Come on, let us climb the LORD's mountain
p: The words of Israel's pilgrim songs are put in the mouths of foreign peoples.
b: Israelites going up to Jerusalem for the feasts sang "Who can climb the LORD's mountain?" (Psalm 24:3) and "Let's go to the LORD's house" (Psalm 122:1). Here other nations sing the pilgrims' song. They come not to bring tribute but to be taught. Christian readers from Justin Martyr on saw the fulfillment in the apostles, who took the word out from Jerusalem to the nations (Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8; Justin, First Apology 39). Jewish readers look for it in the messianic age.

a: For from Zion comes teaching
p: Yoreinu, 'he will teach us', and torah, 'teaching', come from the same root. The synagogue sings this line as the Torah scroll comes out.
b: The pilgrims say 'he will teach (yoreinu) us', and the reason is that torah goes out from Zion: teaching that God gives. 'The LORD's word' in the next line shows that the teaching is prophetic and living, not only written law. In the synagogue, when the ark is opened and the Torah scroll is taken out, the congregation sings this line, ki mitsiyyon tetse torah, so that every Torah reading is heard as this promise being kept.

a: They will pound their swords into plowshares
p: Iron for weapons becomes iron for farming. Joel later turns the saying around (Joel 3:10).
b: In Isaiah's day iron was still costly; a smith could beat a sword into a plow point ('et, perhaps a hoe or mattock) and a spear into a pruning knife for the vines. Joel turns the words around for the day of battle: "Pound your plowshares into swords" (Joel 3:10). Micah adds that each will sit under his own vine and fig tree with no one to make him afraid (Micah 4:4). The verse is cut into the wall of a small park across from the United Nations in New York, and a bronze statue of a man beating a sword into a plow, given by the Soviet Union in 1959, stands in the UN garden.

a: He will be judge between the nations
t: When will the nations stop making war?
p: Jews look to the days of the Messiah; Christians differ on whether it is now, in the church, or after Christ's return.
b: Peace comes because the LORD judges the nations' disputes: their wars end when they accept his rulings. Jewish tradition reads it of the messianic age, when, Maimonides says, there will be no war or famine, and the world will be busy only with knowing the LORD. Early Christians such as Justin Martyr said it was being fulfilled already, because Christians who had once killed each other no longer made war (Dialogue with Trypho 110). Many amillennial readers see a partial fulfillment in the gospel's spread and a full one in the new creation. Premillennial and dispensational readers expect it in Christ's thousand-year reign on earth (Revelation 20:4). Critical scholars read a hope that grew in Israel's worship.

a: let us walk in the LORD's light
p: The prophet turns from the nations' future to Jacob's present: if the nations will walk this way, why not Israel now?
b: The short call of 2:5 hinges between the vision (2:2–4) and the judgment (2:6–22). It takes up the pilgrims' 'we will walk' (2:3) and applies it to Israel today. Light is one of the book's great images: the people in darkness see a great light (9:2), the servant is 'a light for the nations' (42:6; 49:6), and Zion is told, 'Arise, shine, for your light has come' (60:1–3). John's Gospel and First John take up the image of walking in the light (John 8:12; 1 John 1:7).

a: They are crammed with what comes from the East
t: Things from the East, and foreign deals
p: The Hebrew is short and hard. Most read it as foreign religion and fortune-telling filling the land.
b: The Hebrew says only 'they are full from the East' (mikkedem). Many scholars add or change a word to read 'full of diviners from the East' (qesamim), matching 'soothsayers like the Philistines'; the Greek has 'their land is filled, as from the beginning, with divinations'. The last line, 'they make deals with the children of foreigners', renders yaspiqu, which may mean 'clap hands' (strike bargains) or 'abound in'. Under Uzziah and Jotham, Judah prospered from trade (2 Kings 14:22; 2 Chronicles 26:6–10), and with trade came foreign gods and customs. The verse opens by speaking to God: 'You have cast off your people'.
orig: כִּי מָלְאוּ מִקֶּדֶם ... יַשְׂפִּיקוּ (ki male'u miqqedem ... yaspiqu)

a: Horses fill their land
p: The very things the law of the king forbids a king to pile up: horses, and silver and gold.
b: Deuteronomy's law of the king says that the king "must not get himself many horses" and "must not pile up great amounts of silver and gold for himself" (Deuteronomy 17:16–17). Isaiah sees a land full of both, and of idols (2:8). Wealth, war horses and idols go together because all three are things to trust in place of God, as Isaiah will say of the alliance with Egypt (31:1). Under Uzziah Judah was rich and well armed (2 Chronicles 26:6–15).

a: worthless idols
p: 'Elilim sounds like 'elohim, 'gods', and like 'al, 'not'. A sneer: 'godlets', 'no-gods'.
b: 'Elil means 'worthless, nothing' (Job 13:4 'worthless healers'). Isaiah uses it far more than any other book, always of idols (2:8, 18, 20; 10:10–11; 19:1, 3; 31:7). It sounds like a diminutive of 'elohim, 'gods', and like the word 'not': they are not-gods. The verse also sets up the irony of the chapter: people bow down (yishtachavu) to what their hands made, and so 2:9 says they 'bend low', the same humbling that God's day will bring on them (2:11, 17).

a: and you must not pardon them
p: Tissa' means 'lift up' and so 'forgive'. The prophet asks God not to forgive, or not to raise them again.
b: We'al tissa' lahem is literally 'and do not lift (up) for them'. The verb nasa', 'lift', is used for forgiving (lifting away) sin (Genesis 50:17; Exodus 32:32), so most read 'do not forgive them'. Others read 'do not raise them up', since they have just bent low. Either way it is a startling line for a prophet, and some scholars think it is a later scribe's comment. It is missing, with all of 2:10, from the Great Isaiah Scroll (see the variant).

a: away from the dread of the LORD
t: A refrain of the day of the LORD
p: The poem of 2:6–22 is held together by two refrains: hiding from the LORD's dread (2:10, 19, 21) and the LORD alone high (2:11, 17).
b: The first refrain tells people to hide in rocks and dust 'away from the dread of the LORD / and his majestic splendor' (2:10), then describes them doing it (2:19, 21). The second says human pride will be lowered 'and the LORD alone will stand high / on that day' (2:11, 17). The same pair of verbs, 'bend low' and 'be brought down', returns in 5:15. The repetition is the poem's structure: it hammers in one idea, that only one thing in the universe is high.

a: on that day
p: Bayyom hahu' points to the day the LORD acts. Isaiah uses the phrase more than forty times.
b: 'On that day' links an oracle to the coming day of the LORD. In 2:11–20 it is a day of judgment on everything proud; in 4:2 and many later passages (10:20; 11:10–11; 12:1; 25:9; 27:1) it is a day of rescue. Many of the 'on that day' sayings are short prose additions that extend an oracle, and critical scholars often see them as the work of later editors; traditional readers see them as Isaiah's own way of tying his visions together.

a: For a day belongs to the LORD of Armies
p: Amos had already warned that the day of the LORD would be darkness for Israel. Isaiah aims it at all human pride.
b: Israel hoped for 'the day of the LORD' as the day he would defeat its enemies. Amos, a little before Isaiah, turned it around: it will be darkness for Israel (Amos 5:18–20). Isaiah makes it a day against everything high, whether in nature (cedars, mountains) or made by people (towers, walls, ships). Later prophets take up the theme (13:6–13; Joel 2; Zephaniah 1:14–18; Malachi 4:5), and the New Testament speaks of 'the day of the Lord' as Christ's return (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10). Some readers see near fulfillments in Assyria's invasions and a final one at the end; critical scholars read 2:6–22 as a poem that grew over time.
r: Amos 5:18–20; 13:6–13; Joel 2:1–11; Zephaniah 1:14–18; Malachi 4:5; 1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10

a: against all the cedars of Lebanon
p: Trees, mountains, towers, walls and ships: the list moves from God's works to human ones, and all are 'high'.
b: The list runs in pairs: cedars and oaks (the tallest trees of Lebanon and Bashan), mountains and hills, towers and walls, ships of Tarshish and fine ships. Each pair is called 'towering' or 'rising up', the words used of human pride in 2:11–12. The trees are not wicked; they stand for everything that seems great. Uzziah had built towers in Jerusalem and the countryside (2 Chronicles 26:9–10), and Jotham built more (2 Chronicles 27:3–4); Uzziah rebuilt the port of Elath on the Red Sea (2 Kings 14:22). So the list may hit the prosperity of Isaiah's own youth.

a: the ships of Tarshish
t: Ships of Tarshish, and ships people treasure
p: Tarshish ships were large seagoing ships. The parallel phrase is uncertain: 'pleasant pictures' (KJV) or 'fine ships'.
b: Tarshish was a distant port, perhaps Tartessus in Spain or a place in Sardinia, and 'ships of Tarshish' became the name for big ocean-going merchant ships, the way 'East Indiamen' named a class of ship (1 Kings 10:22; 1 Kings 22:48). The parallel sekhiyyot hachemdah is unclear. The KJV's 'pleasant pictures' takes sekhiyyah as 'something to look at'. Words for 'ship' in Ugaritic and Egyptian support the reading 'ships', and the Greek has 'every sight of beauty of ships', so most now read 'fine ships' or 'ships of desire'.
orig: אֳנִיּוֹת תַּרְשִׁישׁ ... שְׂכִיּוֹת הַחֶמְדָּה ('oniyyot Tarshish ... sekhiyyot hachemdah)

a: when he rises up to make the earth tremble in terror
p: La'arots ha'arets: a sound-play, 'to terrify the earth'. An earthquake under Uzziah was long remembered.
b: The verb 'arats, 'terrify, make tremble', echoes 'erets, 'earth'. The people hide in caves 'in the rocks' (tsurim), while the LORD, Israel's true Rock, rises. Isaiah's hearers remembered an earthquake 'in the days of Uzziah' so great that Amos dated his book by it and Zechariah recalled it two centuries later (Amos 1:1; Zechariah 14:5). Revelation pictures people at the end who "hid in caves and among the rocks of the mountains" crying to the rocks to fall on them (Revelation 6:15–16; compare Luke 23:30).

a: out to the moles and the bats
p: The idols are thrown into the dark holes where burrowing animals live, the same holes the people hide in.
b: Lachpor perot is split into two words in the Leningrad Codex ('to the digging of rats'); the Great Isaiah Scroll writes one word, chafarparim, 'moles' or 'shrews'. Bats are unclean animals (Leviticus 11:19). The irony is sharp: people throw their gods into the dark holes of the ground and then crawl into the same holes themselves (2:21). The gold and silver gods they bowed down to end up with the vermin.

a: Stop relying on human beings
p: Human life is a breath God put in the nose (Genesis 2:7). Missing from the Greek.
b: The breath (neshamah) in the nostrils recalls Genesis 2:7, where the LORD God "blew into his nostrils the breath of life". What God breathed in, God can take back. The psalmist says the same: "Do not rely on nobles, / on a son of man, who has no rescue in him" (Psalm 146:3). The verse sums up chapter 2 and leads into chapter 3, where all the leaders people relied on are removed. It is not in the Greek (see the variant), and many scholars think it is a later reader's summary.

a: everything and everyone they lean on
p: Mash'en umash'enah: the same word in a masculine and a feminine form, meaning 'every kind of support'.
b: Hebrew can pair a masculine and a feminine form of a word to mean 'all of it' (like 'one and all'). The 'support' is first food and water, what a city under siege runs out of, and then, in 3:2–3, the leaders a society leans on. The KJV's 'the stay and the staff' keeps the sound-play. Many scholars think 'all their bread ... all their water' was added by a later reader thinking of the siege of 586 BC (2 Kings 25:3; Lamentations 4:4), since 3:2–3 is about people. The verse looks back to 2:22: stop relying on human beings, for God is about to remove them.

a: the warrior and the fighting man
t: A city stripped of its leaders
p: Conquerors took away the elite. In 597 BC Babylon deported Jerusalem's soldiers and craftsmen, as 3:1–3 foresees.
b: Assyria and Babylon broke conquered nations by deporting their leaders and skilled workers and leaving the poor (2 Kings 24:14–16). Sennacherib claims to have taken more than 200,000 people from Judah in 701 BC, and in 597 Nebuchadnezzar "marched all Jerusalem off into exile: every commander, every strong fighting man, ten thousand captives, and every craftsman and smith" (2 Kings 24:14). The list of 3:2–3 is a portrait of Judah's ruling class: soldiers, judges, prophets, elders and officers, but also diviners and spell-casters, whom the law forbids (Deuteronomy 18:10–11). Isaiah lists them without comment as the people the nation actually trusted.

a: the one wise in magic arts
p: Chakham charashim can mean 'a skilled craftsman' or 'one wise in magic'. Nevon lachash is 'expert in whispered spells'.
b: Charashim may be the plural of charash, 'craftsman', so 'a skilled craftsman' (KJV 'the cunning artificer'), which fits the deportation of craftsmen (2 Kings 24:14). Or it may be from cheresh, 'magic', which suits the next phrase. Lachash is a whispered spell, used for charming snakes (Psalm 58:5; Jeremiah 8:17; Ecclesiastes 10:11); the KJV's 'eloquent orator' reflects an older guess. The 'man people look up to' is literally 'lifted of face', a man of rank.
orig: חֲכַם חֲרָשִׁים וּנְבוֹן לָחַשׁ (chakham charashim unevon lachash)

a: spoiled children will rule over them
p: Ta'alulim may mean 'babes' (KJV) or 'caprice, wantonness'. Either way, rulers with no sense.
b: The word comes from a root meaning 'deal with, play with', and elsewhere it means 'mockery' or 'wanton dealings' (66:4). Because it stands beside 'boys', the KJV took it as 'babes', from the similar word 'olel, 'child' (see 3:12). Some readers have thought of Ahaz, who became king at twenty (2 Kings 16:2), or Manasseh, who came to the throne at twelve (2 Kings 21:1); Isaiah speaks more generally of a society that has lost its grown-ups. Ecclesiastes says something similar: 'Woe to you, land, when your king is a boy' (Ecclesiastes 10:16).

a: the worthless will defy the honored
p: Nikleh and nikhbad: 'the light one' and 'the heavy one'. In Hebrew, honor is weight.
b: Nikleh comes from qalal, 'be light, trivial', and nikhbad from kaved, 'be heavy', the root of kavod, 'glory, honor'. A person of honor has 'weight'. The collapse of society is a world turned upside down: the young insult the old (against Leviticus 19:32) and the lightweight push the weighty around. The verb in the first line, nigas, 'push around, oppress', is the word for Pharaoh's slave drivers (Exodus 5:6), and it returns in 3:12.

a: You own a coat! Be our chief!
t: Rule for a man with a coat
p: Owning an outer cloak, a poor man's blanket at night, is enough to be made leader.
b: The simlah was the outer cloak a man wore by day and slept in at night; the law forbade keeping a poor man's cloak overnight as a pledge (Exodus 22:26–27). In the ruined city of 3:6 a man who still owns one is rich enough to rule. The 'pile of rubble' (makhshelah, literally 'a stumbling') plays on 3:8, where Jerusalem 'has tripped' (kashelah). The candidate's answer in 3:7, 'I am no one to bandage wounds', recalls the untreated wounds of 1:6.
orig: שִׂמְלָה לְכָה קָצִין תִּהְיֶה־לָּנוּ (simlah lekhah qatsin tihyeh-lanu)

a: Their faces give them away
t: The look on their faces, or favoritism?
p: Hakkarat peneihem may mean 'the look of their faces' or 'their regard for persons', that is, partiality in court.
b: Hakkarah is from hikkir, 'recognize', and the phrase hikkir panim, 'recognize faces', is the law's term for showing favoritism in judgment: "Do not play favorites" (Deuteronomy 16:19; Deuteronomy 1:17; Proverbs 24:23). Read that way, 3:9 says their partiality in court testifies against them, which suits a chapter about judges and elders. Read the other way, their very expressions show their guilt. Either way they make no attempt to hide their sin, any more than Sodom did (Genesis 19:4–9).

a: They will eat what their own deeds have grown
p: 3:10–11 states the rule of the wisdom books: the righteous eat the fruit of their deeds, and the wicked get what they gave.
b: These two verses sound like Proverbs (Proverbs 1:31; 12:14; 18:20) or Psalm 1, and many scholars think a teacher added them to make the oracle a lesson. They say that God's judgment of Jerusalem is not blind: in a disaster that falls on everyone, the righteous are not forgotten. The book itself complicates the rule: the servant in 53:9 suffers though he did no violence. Paul gives the same rule in Galatians 6:7–8.

a: Those who guide you send you wandering
p: Me'asherekha: 'those who lead you straight', or, as the Greek has it, 'those who call you happy'.
b: The verb 'ishsher can mean 'lead straight' or 'call happy, bless' (the root of 'ashrei, 'happy is'). The Greek reads 'those who call you blessed', flatterers who tell the people all is well. The same pair of words returns in 9:16, where those who lead the people astray swallow them up. 'They have gobbled up the paths you travel' is literally 'they have swallowed the way of your paths': the leaders have made the road disappear.

a: to judge the peoples
p: The Hebrew says 'peoples', but the next verse is about Judah's leaders. The Greek and Syriac read 'his people'.
b: The LORD rises in court against 'the peoples' ('ammim), yet 3:14–15 is addressed to the elders and officials of 'his people'. The Greek has 'his people' ('ammo), as does the Syriac according to BHS, which may be the older reading or may smooth the text. Many keep 'peoples': the LORD is judge of all the earth, and Judah is the first case on his list (compare 2:4). He 'stands' to judge, as judges did in some courts, while in others they sat (Psalm 82:1).

a: You grazed the vineyard bare!
p: Before the song of 5:1–7, the leaders are accused of eating up the vineyard, God's people.
b: Ba'artem means 'you have grazed' or 'burned'; Exodus 22:5 uses it of letting cattle graze in another man's field. The vineyard is the LORD's people, as the song of 5:1–7 will say outright. Those set to guard it have eaten it. The theft is literal too: 'what you stole from the poor' is in their houses. The image of bad shepherds who feed on the flock is close (Ezekiel 34:2–3; Jeremiah 12:10).

a: the Lord GOD of Armies declares
p: Adonai YHWH: 'Lord' and the divine name together. Since YHWH is read 'Adonai', the pair is read 'Adonai Elohim'.
b: When the Hebrew has Adonai ('Lord') followed by YHWH, Jewish readers say Adonai Elohim, 'the Lord God', to avoid saying 'Lord Lord'. English Bibles show this by printing "the Lord GOD" with GOD in capitals. Isaiah uses the fuller 'the Lord GOD of Armies' at 3:15, 10:23–24, 22:5, 12, 14–15 and 28:22. The ne'um, 'declares', stamps the accusation of 3:14–15 as the LORD's own words.

a: Zion's daughters hold themselves high
p: Isaiah turns from the men who rule (3:1–15) to the wealthy women of the city. Both are judged for pride bought with others' poverty.
b: The 'daughters of Zion' here are the women of Jerusalem's ruling families, not the city as a woman ('Daughter Zion', 1:8). Amos made a similar attack on the women of Samaria, the 'cows of Bashan' who crush the poor (Amos 4:1). Isaiah's charge is pride, the sin of 2:11–17 (gavah, 'be high', is the same verb), paraded in the street. The long list of finery in 3:18–23 shows where the plunder of 3:14 went. The poem does not single out women for blame: their husbands are judged first (3:1–15) and fall in war (3:25). Some modern readers find its picture of public shame for women harsh; others note that it is about class as much as gender.

a: the LORD will strip their foreheads bare
p: Pot is rare. Many link it to an Akkadian word for 'forehead'. The KJV has 'their secret parts'.
b: The meaning of pothen is debated. One view, supported by the Akkadian pūtu, 'forehead', reads 'he will lay bare their foreheads', that is, shave their heads, as captives were shaved (compare 3:24 'a shaved head'). The other, followed by the KJV and some modern versions, reads 'their secret parts': conquerors stripped captive women, a common shame in war (20:4; 47:2–3; Nahum 3:5). The parallel line, 'he will make the crowns of their heads scabby', favors the first reading.

a: their little suns and their crescents
p: Many of the 21 items in 3:18–23 appear nowhere else in the Bible. Translations are educated guesses.
b: This is one of the longest lists of women's finery in ancient literature, and translators guess at much of it. Shevisim may be 'little suns', sun-shaped pendants, and saharonim are 'little moons', crescents, like those hung on the necks of Midian's camels (Judges 8:21, 26, where the site also has "the crescents and the drops"). Such pendants were often charms against evil, and crescent and disk pendants have been found in Israel and Judah. The Greek translator, working in Egypt, used the names of jewelry of his own day.

a: the perfume boxes and the charms
p: Batei hannefesh, 'houses of the breath', were probably perfume bottles. Lechashim, 'whisperings', were amulets with a spell.
b: Nefesh means breath, life or self; perfume 'houses' carried the scent. The 'charms' (lechashim, from 'whisper', 3:3) were amulets with a written or spoken spell. Two tiny silver scrolls found in a tomb at Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem, from about 600 BC, were worn this way: rolled up and hung on a cord, they carry a form of the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:24–26), the oldest known copy of a verse of the Bible.

a: a burn scar where beauty was
p: Ki here is a noun, 'branding', perhaps the mark burned onto captives and slaves.
b: The last line is short: ki tachat yofi. Read as a noun (from kavah, 'burn'), ki means a burn or brand: 'branding instead of beauty'. Captives and slaves were sometimes marked this way. The Great Isaiah Scroll adds a word, boshet, 'shame': 'for instead of beauty, shame' (see the variant). The five exchanges of the verse undo the finery of 3:18–23 one by one: perfume, belt, braided hair, gown, beauty.

a: she will be wiped clean and sit in the dirt
t: The widowed city on the ground
p: Zion sits on the ground like a mourner. Roman coins after AD 70 show Judea as a woman seated in mourning.
b: To sit on the ground was the posture of mourning (Job 2:8, 13; Lamentations 2:10). The city that has lost its men (3:25) is pictured as a widow. 'Wiped clean' (nikkatah) means emptied out, cleaned of everything. After Rome took Jerusalem in AD 70, Vespasian struck coins reading IUDAEA CAPTA, 'Judea captured', with a woman seated in mourning under a palm tree; readers have often compared them with this verse and with Lamentations 1:1.

a: seven women will grab hold of one man
p: So many men have died that women beg to marry on any terms, giving up the food and clothing a husband owed a wife.
b: Chapter 4:1 finishes the poem of 3:16–26: the men have fallen (3:25), and the proud women of 3:16 are now desperate. The law said a husband must give his wife food, clothing and marital rights (Exodus 21:10); these women give up the first two if only they may have a husband's name. To have one's name 'called over' something meant to belong to its owner (63:19; Jeremiah 14:9). The 'shame' is that of being a widow or unmarried and childless (Genesis 30:23; 54:4). The chapter division is medieval; the Masoretic paragraph marks join 4:1 to 3:16–26, with no break after 3:26 and a break after 4:1, as do most commentators.

a: the LORD's branch
p: Tsemach is 'what sprouts'. It may be the land's new growth, the surviving remnant, or the Messiah, as the Targum reads it.
b: Tsemach means growth, a shoot, what sprouts from the ground (Genesis 19:25). Three readings: (1) The land's new growth. The parallel line, 'the fruit of the land', suggests crops after the devastation of 1:7, a gift of the LORD to the survivors (Wildberger, Williamson). (2) The remnant itself, the people the LORD plants (60:21; 61:3). (3) The Messiah. Jeremiah calls David's heir 'a righteous branch' (Jeremiah 23:5; Jeremiah 33:15) and Zechariah names him 'Branch' (Zechariah 3:8; Zechariah 6:12); the Targum here reads 'the Messiah of the LORD', and many Christian readers, from the church fathers to Young and Motyer, follow. The Greek has no 'branch' at all (see the variant).

a: will be called holy
p: The survivors receive the name of a holy people: what Israel was always meant to be.
b: At Sinai Israel was told it would be "a kingdom of priests, a holy nation" (Exodus 19:6). After the purging of 4:4, those left in Zion will at last be called 'holy', as the Holy One is holy (6:3). This is the book's first clear word about a holy remnant; 6:13 calls it 'a holy seed', and 62:12 says they will be called 'the Holy People'. Holiness here is a gift that follows cleansing, not a reward.

a: whose name is written down for life
p: A city's list of living citizens becomes God's book of life.
b: Ancient cities kept registers of citizens and families (Nehemiah 7:5; Ezekiel 13:9). To be written 'for life' in Jerusalem is to be counted among the living who will share its future. The image grows into God's own book: Moses asks to be wiped out of "your book that you have written" (Exodus 32:32), a psalm prays that the wicked be "wiped out of the scroll of life" (Psalm 69:28), and Daniel 12:1 and Revelation speak of those whose names are "written in the Lamb's book of life" (Revelation 21:27).
r: Exodus 32:32; Psalm 69:28; Daniel 12:1; Malachi 3:16; Philippians 4:3; Revelation 20:12; Revelation 20:15; Revelation 21:27

a: the filth of Zion's daughters
p: Tso'ah is a blunt word, 'excrement'. It refers back to the women of 3:16 and the blood of 1:15.
b: Tso'ah is the coarsest word Isaiah could use; it means human excrement (Deuteronomy 23:13; Isaiah 36:12; compare Isaiah 28:8). The 'daughters of Zion' whose finery was stripped in 3:16–24 are now washed, and Jerusalem's 'bloodshed' (damim, as in 1:15) is rinsed out. The washing of 1:16, which the people would not do, the Lord now does himself, by judgment.

a: with a spirit of judgment
p: Ruach can mean spirit, wind or breath. A 'spirit of burning' may be a scorching wind that purges.
b: Ruach is God's Spirit, a wind, or breath. A 'spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning' may be God's Spirit acting as judge, or a fiery wind like the desert sirocco that dries and burns. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads 'a spirit (wind) of storm' (sa'ar) for 'burning' (see the variant). John the Baptist's words about one who will baptize 'with the Holy Spirit and fire' (Matthew 3:11–12), with the winnowing that follows, may draw on this verse and on Malachi 3:2–3.
orig: בְּרוּחַ מִשְׁפָּט וּבְרוּחַ בָּעֵר (beruach mishpat uveruach ba'er)

a: the LORD will create
p: Bara', the verb of Genesis 1:1, has only God as its subject. Isaiah uses it 21 times, more than any other book.
b: Bara' is used only of God's action, never of what humans make. Isaiah has it more than any other book, most often in chapters 40–66: God creates the heavens and the earth (40:26; 42:5; 45:18), Israel (43:1, 7, 15), and finally 'new heavens and a new earth' and a new Jerusalem (65:17–18). Here, in the first part of the book, he 'creates' a new presence over Zion. Critical scholars often date 4:2–6 late for this reason, among others; others see Isaiah's own vocabulary. The Greek has 'he will come' (reading uva') instead of 'he will create'.

a: a cloud in the daytime and smoke, and at night the bright light of a blazing fire
p: The cloud and fire that led Israel out of Egypt now rest over the whole of Mount Zion.
b: In the wilderness the LORD went "by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them along the road, and by night in a pillar of fire to light their way" (Exodus 13:21). The cloud covered the tabernacle and filled Solomon's Temple with glory (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:10–11). Here it covers not one building but every place on Mount Zion and every gathering of the people. This is one of the book's first pictures of a new exodus, a theme that grows in chapters 11, 35 and 40–55. The Great Isaiah Scroll's copyist skipped from the first 'by day' to the second (4:6), leaving out the middle of the passage, a common copying slip.

a: for a canopy will cover all the glory
p: Chuppah is the canopy of a bride and groom. Over Zion's glory the LORD spreads a marriage canopy.
b: Chuppah appears elsewhere only for the wedding room or canopy of a bride and groom (Joel 2:16; Psalm 19:5, where the sun comes out 'like a bridegroom from the wedding room'). The Jewish wedding canopy is still called the chuppah. The picture fits the book's later image of Zion as the LORD's bride (62:4–5). 'All the glory' may be the glory of God dwelling over Zion, or Zion's own restored glory, which God shelters.

a: It will be a booth
p: In 1:8 Zion was left like a flimsy booth in a vineyard. Now God himself is Zion's booth.
b: The sukkah of 1:8 was a watchman's shelter left in a ruined field, a picture of abandonment. Here the same word describes the LORD's own shelter over the city, from the heat of day and from storm and rain. Israel's Feast of Booths remembered the shelters of the wilderness (Leviticus 23:42–43), when the LORD led them by cloud and fire, which 4:5 has just recalled. Isaiah 25:4 and 32:2 return to the image of God as shade and shelter.

a: Let me sing for my dear one
t: A love song that becomes a lawsuit
p: Isaiah sings like a friend at a wedding, about his friend's vineyard. Only in 5:7 do the hearers learn the song is about them.
b: In love poetry the vineyard is the beloved (Song of Songs 1:6; 2:15; 8:11–12), and the first hearers may have expected a love song, perhaps at a vintage festival. Isaiah sings for 'my dear one' (yedidi) about 'my love's' (dodi) vineyard. By 5:3 the friend himself speaks and asks the hearers to judge; by 5:6 he commands the clouds, so he must be God; in 5:7 the trap closes. Many scholars call it a juridical parable, like Nathan's story to David (2 Samuel 12:1–7) or the prophet's trap for Ahab (1 Kings 20:39–42): the hearers condemn themselves before they know it (Yee).
r: Song of Songs 1:6; Song of Songs 8:11–12; 2 Samuel 12:1–7; 1 Kings 20:39–42; 27:2–6

a: He broke up its soil, picked out its stones
p: Clearing stones, terracing, planting choice vines, building a tower and cutting a rock press: years of work.
b: The hills of Judah are stony, and the stones cleared from a field became its terrace walls and its watchtower; such terraces and towers still stand in the Judean hills. Soreq was a choice red grape (Jeremiah 2:21; Genesis 49:11). A stone tower, unlike the flimsy booth of 1:8, was a lasting investment, and the yeqev, the vat cut into the rock to catch the juice from the treading floor, meant the owner expected many harvests. Every detail says the owner did all he could (5:4).
r: Jeremiah 2:21; Genesis 49:11; Song of Songs 8:11–12; Matthew 21:33

a: In the middle of it he built a tower
p: Jesus begins the parable of the tenants with Isaiah's vineyard, in the Greek's wording (Mark 12:1; Matthew 21:33).
b: Jesus' parable of the wicked tenants opens with this verse: "He set a hedge around it, dug a pit in it for a winepress and put up a tower" (Matthew 21:33; Mark 12:1; Luke 20:9). The 'hedge' comes from the Greek of 5:2, which adds 'I put a hedge around it' (the Hebrew has the hedge only in 5:5). Jewish readers before and after Jesus took the tower as the Temple and the wine vat as the altar (the Targum of Isaiah; Tosefta Sukkah 3:15), which helps explain why the priests knew the parable was aimed at them (Mark 12:12). In Jesus' version the fault is not in the vines but in the tenants, the leaders, as in 3:14.

a: stinking grapes
p: Be'ushim comes from ba'ash, 'to stink'. The vine was the finest kind, but its fruit rotted.
b: The KJV's 'wild grapes' has shaped how many read the verse, as if the vine had reverted to a wild kind. But be'ushim is from ba'ash, 'stink, be foul' (Exodus 7:18), and means sour, rotten or diseased grapes: bad fruit on a good vine. The Greek has 'thorns', which leads into 5:6. The word sounds a little like 'anavim, 'grapes', so the line ends with a jarring near-rhyme.

a: be the judges, please,
p: From 5:3 the singer stops speaking of his friend and the owner himself speaks in the first person.
b: The song begins in the singer's voice (5:1–2) and then, with no warning, the owner says 'my vineyard' (5:3–6). The hearers, 'people living in Jerusalem, men of Judah', are asked to judge between him and his vineyard. They must agree that he did everything (5:4); a vineyard cannot be put on trial, so they are already judging something else. When the owner gives orders to the clouds (5:6), the mask slips: only God commands the rain (1 Kings 17:1; Amos 4:7).

a: Its hedge: I will tear it out
p: A thorn hedge and a stone wall kept animals and thieves out. Without them the vineyard becomes open pasture.
b: Vineyards were fenced with a thorn hedge (mesukkah) and a stone wall (gader). Removing them lets every passing herd graze and trample (Psalm 80:12–13). The owner does not uproot the vines himself; he takes away his protection and stops caring for them, no pruning, no hoeing, no rain, and the vineyard goes back to thornbush and bramble. Isaiah's later song of the vineyard reverses all of this: "I, the LORD, keep it" (27:2–6).
orig: הָסֵר מְשׂוּכָּתוֹ ... פָּרֹץ גְּדֵרוֹ (haser mesukkato ... parots gedero)

a: look, bloodshed!
p: Mishpat / mishpach and tsedaqah / tse'aqah: the words for what God wanted and what he got sound almost the same.
b: God waited for mishpat, justice, and got mishpach; for tsedaqah, righteousness, and got tse'aqah, an outcry. The bad fruit sounds like the good fruit, as counterfeit justice sounds like justice. Mishpach appears only here; it probably means bloodshed (from a root 'pour out'), though some suggest 'lawlessness'. English cannot carry both plays and the meaning at once; attempts include 'he looked for right, and found riot'. The Greek tried: 'I waited for him to do justice, and he did lawlessness, and not righteousness but a cry'.
orig: לְמִשְׁפָּט וְהִנֵּה מִשְׂפָּח לִצְדָקָה וְהִנֵּה צְעָקָה (lemishpat vehinneh mispach litsdaqah vehinneh tse'aqah)

a: look, an outcry!
p: Tse'aqah is the cry of people wronged, the cry God heard from Israel in Egypt and from Sodom's victims.
b: The 'outcry' is the scream for help of people who are robbed or beaten. God heard it from the Israelites in Egypt (Exodus 3:7, 9), and the law warns that he will hear it from a mistreated widow or orphan (Exodus 22:22–23). It is also the word for the cry against Sodom: "The outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great indeed" (Genesis 18:20). Isaiah has called Jerusalem's rulers 'rulers of Sodom' (1:10); now God hears from Jerusalem what he heard from Sodom.

a: The vineyard of the LORD of Armies
p: The vineyard is one of the Bible's great pictures of God's people, from the Psalms to John 15.
b: Asaph's psalm tells Israel's story as a vine: "A vine from Egypt you dug up and moved" (Psalm 80:8). Hosea calls Israel a lush vine (Hosea 10:1), Jeremiah a choice vine turned wild (Jeremiah 2:21), Ezekiel a vine good only for fire (Ezekiel 15). Isaiah later sings a new vineyard song in which the LORD guards his vineyard night and day (27:2–6). Jesus calls himself 'the real vine' and his Father 'the farmer' (John 15:1), and Christian readers have seen there the vine that bears the fruit Isaiah's vineyard did not.
r: Psalm 80:8–16; Hosea 10:1; Jeremiah 2:21; Ezekiel 15:1–8; Ezekiel 19:10–14; 27:2–6; John 15:1–8

a: Woe to those who string house onto house
p: The first woe is against those who bought up their neighbors' family land, leaving them landless.
b: In Israel's law the land belonged to the LORD and was divided among families: "The land must not be sold for good, because the land is mine" (Leviticus 25:23). A family that fell into debt might lose its fields for a time, but they were to return in the Jubilee (Leviticus 25:10–28). Naboth refused to sell his vineyard to the king for this reason (1 Kings 21:3). In the prosperous 700s the rich bought up small farms and built estates, and the poor became tenants or debt slaves (Micah 2:2; Amos 2:6). Isaiah's punishment fits: the owners of all the houses will live alone in empty houses (5:9).
r: Leviticus 25:10–28; Leviticus 25:23; 1 Kings 21:1–3; Micah 2:1–2; Amos 2:6; Nehemiah 5:1–5

a: In my ears the LORD of Armies has spoken
p: The Hebrew says only 'In my ears the LORD of Armies'. The verb, perhaps 'swore' or 'revealed himself', is understood.
b: Hebrew can leave a verb out, but this is abrupt. 22:14 has the full form: 'the LORD of Armies revealed himself in my ears'. The Greek has 'these things were heard in the ears of the LORD of Sabaoth'. What follows is an oath ('im lo', 'if not...', meaning 'surely', 'I swear'). Isaiah reports what he heard in private and now announces it publicly.

a: a single bath of wine
p: Ten acres of vines give six gallons of wine, and the seed sown gives back only a tenth. The rich estates will fail.
b: An 'acre' (tsemed, 'a yoke') was the land a team of oxen could plow in a day. A bath was about 22 liters, roughly six gallons, a pitiful yield from ten acres of vines. A homer was a donkey's load, about 220 liters, and an ephah one tenth of a homer (Ezekiel 45:11): the farmer would harvest a tenth of what he sowed. The land-grabbers of 5:8 will own estates that produce almost nothing (Haggai 1:6; Deuteronomy 28:38–39).

a: chasing after beer
p: Shekar was beer, mostly from barley. 'Strong drink' (KJV) is traditional, but distilled liquor did not exist.
b: Shekar is usually paired with wine (5:22; 28:7; 29:9). It was mainly grain beer, perhaps also date or fruit wine, but never distilled spirits, which were unknown. The KJV's 'strong drink' made it sound like liquor. Drinking itself is not the charge; the second woe is against people whose whole day, from dawn to dark, is spent in drinking parties while they ignore what God is doing (5:12).

a: Lyre and harp, drum and pipe
p: Rich men held banquets with music and wine. Amos describes the same parties in Samaria.
b: Amos pictures the rich of Samaria lying on ivory couches, eating lambs, singing to the harp and drinking wine by the bowl, untroubled by the ruin of Joseph (Amos 6:4–7). He calls such a gathering a marzeach, a word known from Ugarit and later texts for a feast of a social or religious club. Isaiah's charge is the same: music and wine, and no eyes for 'the LORD's deeds', his work in history, which the prophet sees and announces (5:19; 10:12; 28:21).

a: That is why my people go off into exile
p: Isaiah speaks of exile as if it has happened. Assyria took the north into exile in 732 and 722 BC, and many from Judah in 701.
b: The Hebrew perfect ('has gone into exile') is often used by prophets for what is certain to come. Isaiah saw Tiglath-pileser III deport the people of Galilee in 732 BC (2 Kings 15:29) and Sargon take Samaria's people in 722 (2 Kings 17:6). Sennacherib claims to have deported 200,150 people from Judah in 701, a number many think inflated. The Babylonian exile came a century later (2 Kings 24–25). The cause is 'no knowledge' (1:3): they do not know their God (Hosea 4:6).

a: So Sheol has made its throat wider
t: The swallowing mouth of the dead
p: Sheol opens its throat like a monster. Canaanite poems picture Death (Mot) with one lip on earth and one on the sky.
b: Sheol is the world of the dead. Here it has a nefesh, a throat or appetite, and a mouth opened without limit, and Jerusalem's nobles and crowds go down into it. In the Ugaritic Baal poems the god Mot ('Death') has a lip to the earth and a lip to the heavens, and swallows Baal. Israel did not worship Death, but its poets borrowed the picture of death as an insatiable mouth (Proverbs 30:15–16; Habakkuk 2:5). Isaiah later turns it around: the LORD 'will swallow up death forever' (25:8).

a: the holy God proves that he is holy
p: God's holiness is not only his distance from the world. He shows that he is holy by doing justice.
b: Niqdash means 'shows himself holy, is treated as holy'. In Leviticus and Ezekiel God shows his holiness by acting, often in judgment (Leviticus 10:3; Ezekiel 28:22; Ezekiel 38:16). Isaiah links holiness with justice and righteousness: the holy God is known not by ritual but by setting things right. 'Stands tall' (vayyigbah) uses the same root as the haughty of 5:15 (gevohim): when human height is brought down, only the LORD's remains (2:11, 17).
orig: וְהָאֵל הַקָּדוֹשׁ נִקְדָּשׁ בִּצְדָקָה (veha'el haqqadosh niqdash bitsdaqah)

a: on ropes of nothingness
p: The sinners harness themselves to their guilt and drag it along, like oxen pulling a cart.
b: Shav' means emptiness, falsehood, what is worthless (Exodus 20:7, 'misuse' of the name). The picture is of people who have tied themselves to their sin with cords of lies and haul it behind them like a cart. The Greek has 'as with a long rope'. Sin is something they work hard at, not something that happens to them. In 5:19 the same people mock the prophet's warnings.
orig: בְּחַבְלֵי הַשָּׁוְא וְכַעֲבוֹת הָעֲגָלָה (bechavlei hashshav' vekha'avot ha'agalah)

a: Let the Holy One of Israel bring his plan close
p: The mockers quote Isaiah's own words, 'the Holy One of Israel' and 'his plan', and dare God to act.
b: 'The Holy One of Israel' is Isaiah's name for God (1:4), and 'plan' ('etsah) is his word for what God is doing in history (14:24–27; 28:29; 46:10). The scoffers throw both back at him: if God has a plan, let him hurry up so we can see it. 'Let him get moving' (yemaher yachishah) may echo the name of Isaiah's son, Maher-shalal-hash-baz, 'Quick to the plunder, hurry to the spoil' (8:1–3). Jeremiah heard the same taunt (Jeremiah 17:15), and 2 Peter 3:3–4 answers scoffers who ask where Christ's coming is.

a: Woe to those who say of evil, "It is good,"
p: The fourth woe is against people who reverse moral words, so that wrong is called right.
b: The three pairs, good and evil, dark and light, bitter and sweet, cover morals, perception and taste: these people do not just do wrong; they rename it. The law says the same of judges: "Declaring the wicked innocent and declaring the righteous guilty: / the LORD finds both of them abhorrent" (Proverbs 17:15). Amos speaks of those who turn justice into bitterness (Amos 5:7), and Malachi of those who say evildoers are good in God's eyes (Malachi 2:17).
r: Proverbs 17:15; Amos 5:7; Amos 6:12; Malachi 2:17; Matthew 6:22–23; John 3:19–20

a: wise in their own eyes
p: The fifth woe: those who trust their own cleverness. The royal advisers of Isaiah's day are probably in view.
b: Proverbs warns, "Do not be wise in your own eyes. / Fear the LORD, and stay clear of evil" (Proverbs 3:7). In Isaiah's later chapters the court's wise men advise trusting Egypt against Assyria, and Isaiah says the wisdom of the wise will perish (29:14; 31:1–3). Paul quotes 29:14 and warns the Corinthians against thinking themselves wise (1 Corinthians 1:19; 1 Corinthians 3:18; Romans 12:16).

a: who for a bribe say the wicked are in the right
p: Matsdiqei rasha', 'those who justify the wicked': the judge's sin the law forbids. Paul later says God 'justifies the ungodly'.
b: Hitsdiq means 'declare in the right, acquit'. Judges must acquit the innocent and condemn the guilty (Deuteronomy 25:1); God says, 'I will not acquit the guilty' (Exodus 23:7). These 'heroes' of drinking (5:22) take bribes and turn the verdict around. Paul uses the same legal language, in Greek, when he says God 'justifies the ungodly' who trust him (Romans 4:5), knowing how shocking it sounds next to verses like this one; for Paul, God can do it because of Christ (Romans 3:26).
orig: מַצְדִּיקֵי רָשָׁע עֵקֶב שֹׁחַד (matsdiqei rasha' 'eqev shochad)

a: like straw eaten by a tongue of fire
p: Fire eats the dry stalks above ground, and rot takes the root below. Nothing of the plant is left.
b: A 'tongue of fire' is a flame, as at Pentecost (Acts 2:3). The root and the flower stand for the whole plant, so the whole people (37:31; Amos 2:9; Malachi 4:1). The reason given is not one sin but rejecting God's 'teaching' (torah) and his 'saying' ('imrah). The verb 'treated with contempt' (ni'etsu) is the same as in 1:4: the book's charge against Jerusalem comes back as the conclusion of the woes.

a: and his hand is still stretched out
t: A refrain that belongs to chapter 9
p: This refrain returns four times in 9:8–10:4. Many think 5:25–30 was once part of that poem.
b: The words 'In spite of all this, his anger has not turned back, / and his hand is still stretched out' close each stanza of the poem in 9:8–10:4 (9:12, 17, 21; 10:4). Many scholars, from Duhm on, think 5:25–30 was once the last stanza of that poem and that 10:1–4 was once the last of the woes of chapter 5, and that the two were separated when Isaiah's memoir (6:1–9:7) was set between them. Others see a deliberate frame that the editors built around the memoir. The mountains that 'trembled' may recall the great earthquake under Uzziah (Amos 1:1).

a: He will raise a flag for faraway nations
p: The LORD summons the empire by flag and whistle like a farmer calling bees. Assyria is not yet named.
b: The army of 5:26–30 is Assyria, though it is not named until 7:17–20 and 10:5. Tiglath-pileser III (745–727 BC) built Assyria's first standing professional army, which marched west year after year. The LORD raises a flag (nes) on a hill as a rallying point and 'whistles' (sharaq), as a beekeeper whistles bees out of the hive (7:18). In the second half of the book the same flag is raised to call the exiles home (11:12; 49:22; 62:10).

a: he will whistle for it
p: The verse starts with 'nations' and then turns singular: 'whistle for it', 'it comes'. Many read 'a nation far away'.
b: The Hebrew has laggoyim merachoq, 'for nations far away', and then singular words: 'he will whistle for it', 'here it comes'. Many scholars divide the same letters as legoy mimmerchaq, 'for a nation from far away', as in Jeremiah 5:15 and Deuteronomy 28:49, where one distant nation is sent against Israel. The Greek has plurals throughout ('he will whistle for them ... they come'). Read as it stands, the Hebrew moves from the nations in general to the one the LORD calls out of them, Assyria (7:18; 10:5). The Plain keeps both, as the Hebrew has them.
orig: לַגּוֹיִם מֵרָחוֹק ... וְשָׁרַק לוֹ (laggoyim merachoq ... vesharaq lo)

a: No one in its ranks is weary, no one trips
p: Isaiah paints the Assyrian army as a machine: no stragglers, no loose belts, no broken sandals.
b: Assyrian palace reliefs show disciplined ranks of archers, spearmen and chariots, with belted tunics and laced boots, and Assyrian annals describe marches through mountains and rivers. Isaiah's portrait is meant to terrify: this army cannot be outrun or worn out. Its arrows are sharpened and its bows strung (5:28), its horses' hooves hard as flint, important where horses were not shod, and its chariot wheels spin like a storm. Later the book uses the same words of God's own people: those who hope in the LORD 'will run and not grow weary' (40:31).

a: It has a roar like a lioness
p: Assyrian kings compared themselves to raging lions and hunted lions for sport. Isaiah uses their own image.
b: Royal inscriptions of Assyria often compare the king in battle to a raging lion, and the palace reliefs of Nineveh show kings hunting lions. In Isaiah's picture the lion seizes Judah as its prey and drags it off 'to safety' (veyaflit), out of anyone's reach. Later the book reverses the image: a lion will not frighten the LORD from defending Zion (31:4), and in the new creation 'the lion will eat straw like the ox' (11:7; 65:25).

a: Even the light has gone dark in the clouds
p: Chapter 5 ends in darkness. The memoir that follows ends with light: 'The people walking in darkness have seen a great light' (9:2).
b: The growl of the lion becomes the growl of the sea, an image of chaos (17:12–13), and the land is covered in darkness and distress (choshekh tsar). Amos had warned that the day of the LORD would be darkness and not light (Amos 5:18–20). The same words, darkness and distress, return at 8:22, just before the promise that the people walking in darkness will see a great light (9:2). Readers of the whole book are meant to hear the two passages together.

a: In the year King Uzziah died
p: About 740 BC. The Targum and Rashi read 'the year Uzziah was struck with skin disease' for burning incense in the Temple.
b: Edwin Thiele, whose dates this site uses, puts Uzziah's death in 740/739 BC; other systems range from about 742 to 734. Chronicles tells that the proud king went into the LORD's temple to burn incense, which only priests could do, and was struck with a skin disease (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). The Targum reads 'in the year King Uzziah was struck', and Rashi explains 'died' as 'when he was struck with skin disease', since such a man was counted as dead.
