Isaiah's vision takes place in that same Temple, full of smoke, before the King whom no human may approach without cleansing (6:5–7). The year also marked a turning point in history: Tiglath-pileser III was beginning the campaigns that would bring Assyria to Judah's border.

a: I saw the Lord
p: God told Moses no one can see him and live. The Targum says Isaiah saw 'the glory of the LORD'; John says he saw Christ's glory.
b: The LORD told Moses, "no human being can see me and stay alive" (Exodus 33:20), yet the elders 'saw the God of Israel' (Exodus 24:10) and Micaiah saw the LORD on his throne (1 Kings 22:19). Jewish interpreters handled the tension in different ways: the Targum has 'I saw the glory of the LORD', and the Talmud tells how King Manasseh used this verse to accuse Isaiah of contradicting Moses before he had him killed (Yevamot 49b). John's Gospel says that "Isaiah said this because he had seen his glory, and it was about him that he spoke" (John 12:41), meaning Christ's glory; many church fathers held that the one seen was the Son before his birth.
r: Exodus 33:20; Exodus 24:10; 1 Kings 22:19; John 1:18; John 12:41; Ezekiel 1:26–28; Revelation 4:2

a: high and lifted up
p: Ram venissa': the words Isaiah used for everything God would bring low (2:12–14). Only the LORD is truly high.
b: In 2:12–14 everything 'towering' (ram) and 'rising up' (nissa') is brought low. Here the throne, or the Lord on it, is ram venissa': the only true height in the universe. The pair returns twice more: of the LORD 'who is high and lifted up' (57:15), and, startlingly, of the suffering servant, who will 'rise and be lifted up' (yarum venissa', 52:13). Many readers, Jewish and Christian, see the link as deliberate.

a: the hems of his robe filled the temple
p: Shulav: the skirts or hem of a royal robe. The hem alone fills the great hall of the Temple.
b: Shulim are the lower edges of a garment (Exodus 28:33–34, the high priest's hem). The heikhal is the large main hall of the Temple, about 30 by 10 meters (1 Kings 6:2, 17). If the hem of the robe fills it, the one wearing it is far greater than the building, which is at most his footstool (66:1). The Greek has 'the house was full of his glory', bringing the verse into line with 6:3.

a: Seraphim
p: Seraph means 'burning one'. The same word names the snakes of Numbers 21 and the 'flying seraph' of 14:29 and 30:6.
b: This is the only place in the Bible where seraphim appear in God's presence. The word means 'burning ones'. In Numbers 21:6, 8 it names the 'burning snakes' of the wilderness, and Isaiah speaks twice of a 'flying seraph', a winged serpent (14:29; 30:6). Seals and jar stamps from Judah in the 700s BC show winged cobras (the Egyptian uraeus), some with four wings, guarding a royal name or a sun disk (Keel and Uehlinger). Many scholars think Isaiah's seraphim were pictured as fiery winged serpents, perhaps like the bronze serpent Nehushtan that stood in the Temple until Hezekiah broke it (2 Kings 18:4). The text itself gives them faces, feet, hands and voices, and later Jewish and Christian tradition made them the highest order of angels.

a: with two it covered its feet
p: Even the seraphim cover their faces before God. 'Feet' may be a modest word for the body.
b: Moses covered his face, "for he was afraid to gaze at God" (Exodus 3:6), and Elijah wrapped his face in his cloak (1 Kings 19:13). The seraphim do the same. 'Feet' is sometimes a modest word for the private parts in Hebrew (Exodus 4:25; Ruth 3:7; 7:20), so covering the feet may mean covering the body out of reverence; others take it literally. With the third pair of wings they 'would fly', or hover, ready for service (6:6).

a: Holy, holy, holy
p: Hebrew repeats a word to make it superlative. Jews sing these words daily in the Kedushah; Christians in the Sanctus.
b: Saying a word three times is the Hebrew way of saying 'most' (Jeremiah 7:4; Jeremiah 22:29; Ezekiel 21:27): the LORD is utterly holy. The Targum expands it: holy in the highest heavens, holy on earth, holy for ever and ever. Jews say the verse daily in the Kedushah of the morning prayers and the Amidah. Christians sing it in the Sanctus of the Eucharist, a use already hinted at in 1 Clement 34:6–7 (about AD 96). Revelation has the living creatures sing "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty" (Revelation 4:8). Many church fathers saw the Trinity in the threefold 'holy'; Origen reports that his Hebrew teacher took the two seraphim as the Son and the Holy Spirit (On First Principles 1.3.4). The verse itself does not teach the Trinity, but Christian worship has long sung it that way.
r: Revelation 4:8; Jeremiah 7:4; Jeremiah 22:29; Ezekiel 21:27; Psalm 99:3; Psalm 99:5; Psalm 99:9; 57:15

a: Everything that fills the earth is his glory
p: The Hebrew says 'the fullness of the whole earth is his glory'. Most versions say 'the whole earth is full of his glory'.
b: Melo' kol-ha'arets is a noun phrase, 'the fullness of all the earth', as in 'the earth and its fullness' (Psalm 24:1). Read closely, the seraphim say that everything that fills the earth is God's glory, or shows it. Most translations, the Greek and the Christian Sanctus ('heaven and earth are full of your glory') take it as 'the whole earth is full of his glory', which comes to much the same. The temple is full of his robe; the earth is full of his glory (Numbers 14:21; Psalm 72:19; Habakkuk 2:14).

a: smoke kept filling the house
p: Smoke, like the cloud at Sinai and at the Temple's dedication, hides God's glory while showing that he is there.
b: At Sinai the mountain was wrapped in smoke because the LORD came down in fire (Exodus 19:18). When Solomon's Temple was dedicated, "the cloud filled the LORD's house" and the priests could not stand to serve (1 Kings 8:10–11). Revelation sees the heavenly temple "filled with smoke from the glory of God", so that no one could enter (Revelation 15:8). The smoke may also be the incense of the Temple service, the incense Uzziah had wrongly offered (2 Chronicles 26:16).

a: I am finished
p: Nidmeiti may come from a verb 'be destroyed' or from one meaning 'be silent'. The Latin reads 'I kept silent'.
b: Two Hebrew verbs are spelled damah: one means 'be cut off, be destroyed' (Hosea 4:5–6), the other 'be silent'. Most modern versions read 'I am ruined'. The Latin Vulgate has tacui, 'I kept silent', and some modern scholars prefer 'I am struck dumb', which suits a man whose lips are unclean while the seraphim sing. The Greek has 'I am pierced to the heart'. The KJV's 'I am undone' keeps both senses.

a: with my own eyes I have seen the King
p: In the year the earthly king died, Isaiah sees the real King. This is the first time he calls the LORD 'the King'.
b: Isaiah's terror is that he, an unclean man among an unclean people, has seen the King, the LORD of Armies. The title 'King' sets the vision against the death of Uzziah (6:1): the throne of Judah may be empty, but the throne of the universe is not. The book often calls the LORD King (33:17, 22; 41:21; 43:15; 44:6). The Targum says Isaiah saw 'the glory of the Shekhinah of the eternal King'. The Talmud tells that King Manasseh condemned Isaiah for saying he had seen God, since Moses said no one can (Exodus 33:20; Yevamot 49b).

a: a hot stone
p: Ritspah is a glowing stone or coal. Orthodox liturgy and John of Damascus saw in it the bread of Communion.
b: Ritspah is related to the word for a stone pavement; it may be a hot stone used for baking (1 Kings 19:6 has the same root) or a live coal. The altar is probably the incense altar inside the Temple, whose coals were carried with tongs (Leviticus 16:12). The Greek has anthrax, 'a coal'. John of Damascus compared the Eucharist to Isaiah's coal: bread joined with divine fire, which cleanses those who receive it (Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith 4.13). In the Orthodox Divine Liturgy the priest says the words of 6:7 after receiving Communion.

a: atonement is made for your sin
p: The coal touches the lips that were unclean (6:5). The guilt goes; atonement is made. Then Isaiah can speak.
b: Kipper is the regular word for making atonement in the Temple law (Leviticus 4:20; 16:30). Here no animal is offered: fire from the altar cleanses directly, and God acts first, before Isaiah offers to go (6:8). The touching of the mouth recalls other commissions: the LORD touched Jeremiah's mouth to put his words in it (Jeremiah 1:9), and Ezekiel ate a scroll (Ezekiel 3:1–3). In the book's second half the same pair of words, guilt and sin, is taken away from the whole people (40:2; 53:5–6).
orig: וְסָר עֲוֺנֶךָ וְחַטָּאתְךָ תְּכֻפָּר (vesar 'avonekha vechatta'tekha tekhuppar)

a: Who will go for us?
p: Why 'us'? The LORD may be speaking to his heavenly court, as in 1 Kings 22. Many church fathers heard the Trinity.
b: God asks 'Whom am I to send?' (singular) and then 'Who will go for us?' (plural). Three explanations are given. (1) The heavenly council: the LORD is surrounded by his court, as in Micaiah's vision, "I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the army of heaven standing beside him" (1 Kings 22:19), where he also asks for a volunteer (1 Kings 22:20). (2) A plural of deliberation, like 'Let us make' (Genesis 1:26). (3) The Trinity, as many church fathers read it, linking 'us' with the threefold 'holy'. Most modern scholars, Jewish and Christian, prefer the first. The Greek has 'who will go to this people?', with no 'us', so the Trinitarian reading was made from the Hebrew and the Latin (quis ibit nobis).
r: 1 Kings 22:19–22; Genesis 1:26; Genesis 3:22; Genesis 11:7; Job 1:6; Psalm 82:1

a: Here I am! Send me.
p: Hinneni is how Abraham, Moses and Samuel answered God. Isaiah volunteers, unlike Moses and Jeremiah.
b: Abraham ("Here I am", Genesis 22:1), Moses (Exodus 3:4) and Samuel (1 Samuel 3:4) answer God with hinneni. Isaiah alone offers himself before he knows what the task is. Moses begged God to send someone else (Exodus 4:13), and Jeremiah protested that he was too young (Jeremiah 1:6). The verse has inspired many missionaries and the hymn 'Here I Am, Lord' (Dan Schutte, 1981). The task that follows (6:9–13) shows that the volunteer did not know how hard it would be.

a: Listen and listen, but do not understand
t: The most quoted verse of Isaiah in the New Testament
p: 6:9–10 is quoted or echoed in all four Gospels, in Acts and in Romans, to explain why many did not believe.
b: Jesus applies it to the crowds who heard his parables (Matthew 13:13–15; Mark 4:12; Luke 8:10). John uses it for the unbelief that met Jesus' signs: "He has made their eyes blind and their heart hard, so they would not see with their eyes, or understand with their heart, and turn back for me to heal them" (John 12:40). Paul quotes it to the Jewish leaders in Rome (Acts 28:26–27) and echoes it in Romans 11:8, which joins Deuteronomy 29:4 to Isaiah 29:10. Matthew and Acts follow the Greek, which turns the commands into a description: 'this people's heart has grown fat'. Mark's 'and it be forgiven them' agrees with the Targum ('and it be forgiven them') against the Hebrew 'and be healed'.
r: Matthew 13:13–15; Mark 4:11–12; Luke 8:10; John 12:39–41; Acts 28:25–28; Romans 11:7–10; Deuteronomy 29:4

a: Make this people's heart fat
t: Does God want them not to repent?
p: The commission seems to say Isaiah must make the people unable to turn. Readers have explained it in several ways.
b: A 'fat' heart is a dull, unfeeling one (Psalm 119:70); 'heavy' ears are deaf; eyes 'pasted shut' are blind. (1) Result stated as purpose. Hebrew often states the outcome as if it were the aim: Isaiah's preaching will in fact harden them, and God tells him so in advance so he will not lose heart (Calvin; many modern commentators). (2) Judicial hardening. After long refusal (1:2–5; 5:1–7), God confirms the people in the choice they have made, as with Pharaoh (Exodus 9:12). (3) A limited time. 'How long?' (6:11) shows the hardening is for a period, until judgment has done its work; Paul likewise says Israel's hardening is partial and temporary (Romans 11:25). The Greek and the Targum soften the verse.

a: and turn back, and be healed
p: Shuv, 'turn back, return, repent', is the word in the name of Isaiah's son Shear-jashub, 'A remnant will turn back' (7:3).
b: Shuv is the Hebrew Bible's main word for repentance: turning around and coming back to God. It is the root of 'those in her who turn back' (1:27) and of the name of Isaiah's son Shear-jashub, 'A remnant will return' (7:3; 10:21–22). The healing is the healing the body of 1:5–6 needed and never received. In 6:13 the same verb, translated 'again', may also hint that the tenth will 'turn back'.

a: Lord, how long?
p: Isaiah answers with the question of the lament psalms. The answer is: until the land is empty.
b: 'How long?' is the cry of the psalms of lament: "And you, LORD, how long?" (Psalm 6:3; Psalm 13:1; Psalm 74:10; Psalm 90:13), and of the martyrs in Revelation (Revelation 6:10). Isaiah does not refuse his task; he asks how long the hardening will last. The answer reaches as far as the exile: cities ruined, houses empty, the people moved far away (6:12). Readers in the Babylonian exile heard their own situation here, and the second half of the book answers them: Jerusalem's time of service is over (40:2).
r: Psalm 6:3; Psalm 13:1–2; Psalm 74:10; Psalm 90:13; Revelation 6:10; 40:2; Jeremiah 4:14

a: And though a tenth is still left in it
t: The hardest verse of the chapter
p: Almost every word of 6:13 can be read more than one way. Is the tenth burned again, or does it return?
b: The Hebrew is very compressed. Veshavah can mean 'it will again (be burned)' or 'it will turn back, return'. Leva'er can mean 'to be burned' or 'to be grazed'. Matsevet is 'what stands', a stump, but the same word names Absalom's memorial pillar (2 Samuel 18:18), and some see here the standing stones of a shrine under sacred trees (1:29). The Great Isaiah Scroll has two different letters: mishlekhet, 'cast down', for 'in the felling', and bamah, which some read 'high place', for 'in them'. Most read the verse as a second judgment on the survivors of the first, ending in a stump that is a holy seed.
orig: וְשָׁבָה וְהָיְתָה לְבָעֵר ... מַצֶּבֶת (veshavah vehayetah leva'er ... matsevet)

a: Its stump is a holy seed
p: A hope at the end of the darkest commission. Missing from the Greek; many think a later hand added it, others that it is Isaiah's own.
b: The stump of a felled terebinth or oak can sprout again (Job 14:7–9). The 'holy seed' is the remnant from which a new people will grow, the opposite of the 'seed of evildoers' of 1:4 and the shoot that will grow from Jesse's stump (11:1). The only other place the phrase occurs is Ezra 9:2, where "the holy seed has mingled with the peoples of the lands": the returned exiles saw themselves as this seed. The Greek lacks the line (see the variant), and many critical scholars think it was added after the exile; Oswalt, Motyer and others see it as Isaiah's own, matching the remnant hope he gave his son's name (7:3).
